title: Two's complement

milestone.title: Binary: The Language of the Machine

description:
Bit patterns are strings of `0` and `1`, all with the same length. Write:

```python
def add_bits(a, b)          # adds two equal-length patterns like a CPU: same length out, the last carry is dropped
def negate(pattern)         # two's complement: flip every bit, then add one
def signed_value(pattern)   # reads a pattern as a signed number: the top bit is worth minus its usual value
```

- `add_bits("01011", "00111")` is `"10010"` (11 + 7 = 18).
- `add_bits("11111111", "00000001")` is `"00000000"`: overflow, the 9th bit is lost.
- `negate("00000101")` is `"11111011"` (−5), and `negate("11111011")` is `"00000101"`.
- `signed_value("11111011")` is −5, `signed_value("01111111")` is 127, `signed_value("10000000")` is −128.

`reversed(text)` goes through a string backwards (handy for adding from the right). `"".join(list_of_characters)` glues characters into a string. `for x, y in zip(a, b):` walks two strings side by side, a pair of characters at a time, and `int("1")` is the number 1. `if pattern[0] == "1":` runs the indented lines below it only when the top bit is 1; `else:` gives the other branch.
hints: `signed_value`: read the pattern as an ordinary unsigned number first. If the top bit is 1, subtract 2 to the power of the length: for 8 bits, 251 − 256 = −5.
